newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tokyo shares fall sharply on economy, Asia mixed.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo shares fall sharply on economy, Asia mixed.

text.p: Tokyo stocks dropped more than two percent on Japan's economic prospects on Tuesday, but most other Asian markets were mixed in quiet trade ahead of the Christmas holiday.
Brokers said the Tokyo market was jittery about Japan's uncertain economic outlook for 1997, despite optimistic comments from government officials about the nation's economic recovery.

The benchmark Nikkei average of 225 leading shares slid a hefty 528.75 points, or 2.69 percent, to close at 19,161.71. This was its lowest level since December 19, 1995, when the stock index recorded an intraday low of 19,077.12.

Tokyo stocks have been battered by a sell-off that took hold last week when the government confirmed it would tighten fiscal policy next year to tackle the nation's budget deficit, with possible harmful effects on the economy.

"The biggest reason in the current sharp fall is a gap between the market's and the government's perceptions of the economy," said Hiroyuki Nakai, chief investment strategist at Nikko Securities Co Ltd.
Elsewhere in Asia, the upcoming holiday dampened trade activity.
Hong Kong stocks closed a half-day session slightly up in active trade, with year-end demand for the market's leaders giving the index a small boost, brokers said.
The Hang Seng Index rose 10.13 points, or 0.08 percent, to end at 13,341.61 after swinging through a 136-point range.

Thai stocks rallied to finish with modest gains after speculators moved in ahead of monthly economic data due on Thursday, traders said. The SET Index closed up 6.93 points, or 0.85 percent, at 826.72 on sluggish, holiday-thinned, three billion baht turnover.
"The market is up a bit thanks to retail investors although most of our clients are already away for Christmas," said a trader at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Manila stocks ended higher as news that President Fidel Ramos was up on his feet a day after undergoing surgery boosted sentiment, brokers said. The main index ended 12.61 points, or 0.40 percent, up at 3,152.53.

Taiwan share prices ended slightly higher for its fourth consecutive rise, and brokers said they expected a firming trend through the year-end. The index ended up 3.72 points, or 0.05 percent, at 6,935.72, off a 6,964.24 high.

Late buying of heavyweights Tenaga Nasional and Telekom Malaysia pushed the key Kuala Lumpur share market index higher at the close. The Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks ended 11.54 points, or 0.96 percent, higher at 1,209.32.
Singapore's Straits Times Industrials Index closed down 8.72 points, or 0.40 percent, at 2,187.14. Jakarta share prices ended down 0.05 percent on profit taking.

The Seoul bourse ended trading lower as disappointment spread due to a lack of aggressive buying by public pension funds, brokers said. The composite stock index fell 7.05 points, or 1.03 percent, to provisionally close at 677.76.
Australia's benchmark All Ordinaries index and New Zealand's NZSE 40 Capital Index closed up slightly.
February Brent on SIMEX was quoted at $23.20/$23.30 per barrel at the 0800 GMT close, near the London settlement price of $23.19.
The Nikkei's slide lifted the dollar against the yen in late Tokyo. At 1016 GMT, the dollar traded at 114.32/37 yen and 1.5547/52 marks.
Hong Kong gold bullion ended at US$368.90/369.40 an ounce against New York's US$368.60/369.10 close on Monday.
